prompt: By the lesson, what does every software method bet on?
hint: Look at the heading 'Every method is a bet'.

choices.text: Whether the developers are senior enough to work alone
choices.why: Seniority matters, but no method in the course is built on it.

choices.text: Which tool the team uses to track its work
choices.why: A tool records the answer; it does not choose it.

choices.text: How much of the work can be known before it starts
choices.why: Right. A plan up front pays off only when the work can be known up front.

choices.text: How many meetings a team can afford each week
choices.why: Meetings are a consequence of the bet, not the bet itself.

prompt: Two developers agree over coffee that one does the database and the other the screens. Do they have a process?
hint: The lesson's three questions are who decides, in what order, and how outsiders find out.

choices.text: No, because nobody in a manager's role decided anything
choices.why: Who decides can be the two of them; a manager is not required for a process to exist.

choices.text: Yes, an unwritten one that breaks when somebody joins
choices.why: Right. They answered who does what; nothing records it, so a third person or a date request breaks it.

choices.text: Only if they hold a daily meeting about it
choices.why: A daily meeting is one ceremony of one method, not the definition of a process.

choices.text: No, a process needs written documents that somebody signed off
choices.why: Writing it down helps, but the agreement is already a process.

prompt: What did Royce say, in 1970, about the straight sequence of phases he drew first?
hint: He drew it, and then criticised it in the same paper.

choices.text: That it was risky and invited failure
choices.why: Right. Testing came last, so everything wrong arrived at the end; he added feedback and asked for the work to be done twice.

choices.text: That it was the method every large project should follow
choices.why: That is how the figure was later read, without the text around it.

choices.text: That it only suited projects with fixed prices
choices.why: Contracts come up in this lesson, but Royce's objection was about testing coming last.

choices.text: That it should be called the waterfall model
choices.why: The word is not in the paper; it was attached later.

prompt: Which conditions make a plan made up front a reasonable bet? Choose all that apply.
hint: The lesson lists three.

choices.text: The technology is new to the people building it
choices.why: New technology means the team will learn as it goes, which a fixed plan cannot absorb.

choices.text: Users can try a partial version and react
choices.why: That favours short loops: their reactions would change the plan.

choices.text: The requirements are fixed by something outside the team
choices.why: Yes: a law or an existing machine will not change because the team learned something.

choices.text: A late change is very expensive
choices.why: Yes: then getting it right early is worth a lot of effort.

prompt: A sequential project's test phase finds that a requirement was misunderstood in month one. Why is this the model's characteristic failure?
hint: Think about when the system is first exercised as a whole.

choices.text: Testing is the first time the whole runs, so early mistakes surface last
choices.why: Right. Every phase built on the misunderstanding, and nothing could reveal it until everything existed.

choices.text: The requirements document was too short
choices.why: A longer document can be just as wrong; length does not reveal a misunderstanding.

choices.text: Sequential projects skip testing to save time
choices.why: They test; the problem is that they test at the end.

choices.text: The testers were brought in too late to read the requirements
choices.why: Who reads the document does not change when the system can first be exercised.

prompt: Match each plan to how its first delivery looks.
hint: The lesson's figure has three rows.

pairs.right: One finished piece of the product
A rough version of the whole
A thin working slice, screen to database

prompt: What risk does a purely incremental plan leave open?
hint: Each piece is finished before the next starts.

choices.text: That the split was wrong
choices.why: Right. A later piece may break an assumption a finished piece was built on, and the finished piece is reopened.

choices.text: That nothing is finished for a long time
choices.why: That is the iterative plan's risk; incremental finishes pieces early.

choices.text: That the client cannot use any part of the product early
choices.why: The client can use the first piece early; that is the plan's advantage.

choices.text: That testing happens only at the very end of the project
choices.why: Each piece is tested as it is finished.

prompt: Each turn of Boehm's spiral starts with one question. Which one?
hint: The spiral made risk the driver of the loop.

choices.text: Which feature will the users like most when it ships?
choices.why: Value matters, but the spiral orders work by risk.

choices.text: What is the riskiest thing we do not know yet?
choices.why: Right. The turn is spent reducing that risk, so the unknowns that could sink the project are met while changing course is cheap.

choices.text: How much of the budget is left?
choices.why: Budget is checked, but it is not what starts the turn.

choices.text: Which phase of the plan comes next, and who signs it off?
choices.why: That is the sequential model's question.

prompt: What does the sentence that closes the manifesto's four values say about the items on the right, such as documentation?
hint: It is the sentence usually left out.

choices.text: They should be produced at the end of the project
choices.why: The manifesto does not schedule anything.

choices.text: They matter only in regulated industries
choices.why: The manifesto says nothing about industries.

choices.text: They should be dropped by any team that wants to be agile
choices.why: That is the misreading the sentence exists to prevent.

choices.text: They have value; the left is valued more
choices.why: Right. Each line is a preference when the two collide, not a rejection of the right-hand item.

prompt: A colleague says 'agile requires a daily stand-up'. What is the accurate version?
hint: The manifesto names no ceremony.

choices.text: It is accurate as said
choices.why: No ceremony is named in the manifesto.

choices.text: Scrum requires a daily meeting; the manifesto names none
choices.why: Right. Dropping a ceremony may break a Scrum rule, but it breaks no agile value.

choices.text: The manifesto lists the daily stand-up among its twelve principles
choices.why: The principles mention working together daily, not a meeting.

choices.text: Kanban invented the daily stand-up in 2001
choices.why: Neither the date nor the method fits.

prompt: Which of the twelve principles does the lesson single out as the most ignored, and the one an architect should quote?
hint: It connects design to agility.

choices.text: Deliver working software frequently
choices.why: Quoted constantly; it is where the sprint comes from.

choices.text: Business people and developers work together daily
choices.why: Scrum turns it into a role, so it is hardly ignored.

choices.text: Continuous attention to technical excellence and good design
choices.why: Right. Without it, welcoming late change stops being affordable.

choices.text: Welcome changing requirements
choices.why: Well known; the lesson notes it is expensive to honour.

prompt: The manifesto says working software is the primary measure of ___.
hint: A status report of 80% is not it.

prompt: At the initial idea, the cone says real effort lands between a quarter and how many times the estimate?
hint: The widest end of the cone.

prompt: A project has run for six months without deciding which integrations it will support. Where is it on the cone?
hint: What narrows the cone?

choices.text: Exactly halfway, at half to double
choices.why: That range belongs to a defined product, which this one is not.

choices.text: Still near the wide end
choices.why: Right. The cone narrows when decisions remove variability, not when months pass.

choices.text: Outside the cone entirely, at a point it does not cover
choices.why: The cone covers every stage; the project sits at the stage its decisions reached.

choices.text: At the narrow end, because six months have passed
choices.why: That is the wrong reading the lesson names: time alone narrows nothing.

prompt: Kent Beck's 1999 argument changes which part of the case for planning up front?
hint: If late change were cheap...

choices.text: The claim that requirements can be written down
choices.why: Beck's argument is about the cost of change, not about writing.

choices.text: The exact multipliers of the cost-of-change curve
choices.why: Questioning the multipliers is Bossavit's work, from 2012.

choices.text: The width of the cone of uncertainty at the initial idea
choices.why: The cone measures estimates, which Beck did not dispute.

choices.text: The premise that late change must stay expensive
choices.why: Right. Tests, simple design and integration flatten the curve, and then planning everything first loses its reason.

prompt: What did Bossavit find when he traced the most quoted cost-of-change multipliers?
hint: The direction of the claim survived; something else did not.

choices.text: That late changes are cheaper than early ones
choices.why: He did not reverse the direction; he questioned the precise numbers.

choices.text: Much thinner evidence than their popularity suggests
choices.why: Right. Often one old study, quoted at second or third hand.

choices.text: That the multipliers are exactly right and were confirmed by later studies
choices.why: That is the opposite of his finding.

choices.text: That Boehm never measured anything and invented the curve
choices.why: Boehm measured; the trouble was in how the figures were passed on.

prompt: A clinic network wants online booking: receptionists can try early screens, the payment provider's API is fixed by contract, and old appointments must be migrated with no way back. What does the lesson suggest?
hint: Each part has its own conditions.

choices.text: Run everything in two-week sprints, since there are users
choices.why: The migration cannot be undone, and short loops do not change that.

choices.text: Plan the whole project sequentially, since one part is fixed
choices.why: The screens have users who can react; a fixed plan wastes that.

choices.text: Pick whichever method the team used last time
choices.why: The lesson's point is that the work, not habit, should decide.

choices.text: A dated plan for the fixed parts, short loops for the rest
choices.why: Right. Each part gets the bet its conditions support.

prompt: Match each contract to what it fixes.
hint: One of them fixes nothing but the rate.

pairs.right: Only the rate for the effort spent
Budget and date, leaving scope open

prompt: In Cynefin's terms, what is a complex problem?
hint: Compare it with complicated.

choices.text: A problem with no answer at all
choices.why: Complex problems have answers; they are found by experiment.

choices.text: Any problem that needs more than one team
choices.why: Size is not the distinction Cynefin draws.

choices.text: One with a right answer an expert can find in advance
choices.why: That is a complicated problem.

choices.text: One whose answer only emerges from trying things
choices.why: Right. The system reacts to what you do, so the plan becomes a series of experiments.

prompt: A team holds every Scrum ceremony, but does requirements in sprint 1, design in sprint 2 and testing in sprint 7. What is it, by the lesson's test?
hint: Is there working software at the end of each cycle?

choices.text: A sequence with shorter labels
choices.why: Right. Nothing works until the end, so the fortnights are phases.

choices.text: An agile team, since it holds the ceremonies
choices.why: Ceremonies do not make work iterative; working software each cycle does.

choices.text: A Kanban team that has not noticed it yet
choices.why: Nothing about flow or limits is described.

choices.text: An iterative team, because the sprints repeat
choices.why: Repeating a calendar is not revisiting a product.

prompt: What do agile methods do about planning, according to the lesson?
hint: More often, or less?

choices.text: They plan every cycle, with little detail far ahead
choices.why: Right. Detail months away is mostly invented, so it is left rough.

choices.text: They skip planning and respond to change instead
choices.why: That is the misreading this section opens with.

choices.text: They plan once, in detail, at the start
choices.why: That describes the sequential bet.

choices.text: They leave planning to the product owner alone
choices.why: The team plans together each sprint.

prompt: Put the phases of the classic sequence in order.
hint: Each one hands a document to the next.
trap: Verification comes after implementation: it tests the code that exists.

prompt: Order these stages from the widest range of estimate error to the narrowest.
hint: The cone narrows as decisions are made.
trap: A defined product (half to double) is still wider than finished requirements (about two thirds to one and a half).

prompt: A client asks for a fixed price on a product whose users have not seen anything yet. Which risk is the client really asking the supplier to carry?
hint: Where is the product on the cone?

choices.text: No risk at all, since the price was agreed and signed before the work
choices.why: Agreeing a price moves the risk; it does not remove it.

choices.text: The risk of the users disliking the colours
choices.why: A real risk, and a small one next to the estimate's range.

choices.text: The uncertainty of an estimate made at the wide end of the cone
choices.why: Right. A fixed price fixes a number taken where the range is widest.

choices.text: The risk of the team using sprints
choices.why: How the team works inside the contract is not what the price fixes.

prompt: Incremental adds finished pieces; ___ revisits the whole product, round after round.
hint: The other of the two words.
